Complex exponential integral means spectra of univalent functions and the Brennan conjectureThanks: The author was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 11501157).

Jianjun Jin Address: School of Mathematics, Hefei University of Technology, Xuancheng Campus, Xuancheng 242000, P.R.China Email address: jin@hfut.edu.cn, jinjjhb@163.com
Abstract.

In this paper we investigate the complex exponential integral means spectra of univalent functions in the unit disk. We show that all integral means spectrum (IMS) functionals for complex exponents on the universal Teichmüller space, the closure of the universal Teichmüller curve, and the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space are continuous. We also show that the complex exponential integral means spectrum of any univalent function admitting a quasiconformal extension to the extended complex plane is strictly less than the universal integral means spectrum. These extend some related results in our recent work [39]. Here we employ a different and more direct approach to prove the continuity of the IMS functional on the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space. Additionally, we completely determine the integral means spectra of all univalent rational functions in the unit disk. As a consequence, we show that the Brennan conjecture is true for this class of univalent functions. Finally, we present some remarks and raise some problems and conjectures regarding IMS functionals on Teichmüller spaces, univalent rational functions, and a multiplication operator whose norm is closely related to the Brennan conjecture.

Key words and phrases: 
Complex exponential integral means spectrum of univalent function, universal integral means spectrum, Brennan conjecture, univalent function with a quasiconformal extension, univalent rational function, univalent polynomial, universal Teichmüller space, universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, universal Teichmüller curve

1. Introduction

Let Δ={z:|z|<1}\Delta=\{z:|z|<1\} be the unit disk in the complex plane ℂ\mathbb{C}. We denote by ℂ^=ℂ∪{∞}\widehat{\mathbb{C}}=\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\} the extended complex plane and let ℝ\mathbb{R} be the real line. For a complex number zz, we use arg⁡z\arg z to denote the unique argument of zz satisfying that argz∈(−π,π]\arg z\in(-\pi,\pi]. Let Ω\Omega be a bounded simply connected domain in ℂ\mathbb{C} with 0∈Ω0\in\Omega. Let ff be an analytic function in Ω\Omega with f⁡(0)=1f(0)=1 and f⁡(z)≠0f(z)\neq 0 for all z∈Ωz\in\Omega. In this paper, we always use log⁡f\log f to denote the unique single-valued branch of the logarithm of ff in Ω\Omega with arg⁡f⁡(0)=0\arg f(0)=0.

We denote by 𝒰\mathcal{U} the class of all univalent functions (conformal mappings) in Δ\Delta. We let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the class of all univalent functions ff in Δ\Delta with f⁡(0)=f′​(0)−1=0f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)-1=0 and let 𝒮b\mathcal{S}_{b} be the subclass of 𝒮\mathcal{S} which consists of all bounded univalent functions.

Let τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}. The integral means spectrum βf​(τ)\beta_{f}(\tau) for f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S} is defined as

(1.1) βf​(τ):=lim supr→1−log∫−ππ|[f′(rei​θ)]τ|dθ|log⁡(1−r)|.\beta_{f}(\tau):=\limsup_{r\rightarrow 1^{-}}\frac{\log\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|[f^{\prime}(re^{i\theta})]^{\tau}|d\theta}{|\log(1-r)|}.
Remark 1.1.

For f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S}, since f′​(z)f^{\prime}(z) is never zero in Δ\Delta and f′​(0)=1f^{\prime}(0)=1, we define the complex power [f′​(z)]τ[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau} as

[f′​(z)]τ=exp⁡(τ​log⁡f′​(z)).[f^{\prime}(z)]^{\tau}=\exp(\tau\log f^{\prime}(z)).

For real τ\tau, the integral means measure the boundary expansion and compression associated with a given conformal map. Allowing τ\tau to be a complex exponent, we should also take into account the rotation.

The universal integral means spectra B⁡(τ)B(\tau) and Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau) are defined as

B⁡(τ)=supf∈𝒮βf​(τ)​and​Bb​(τ)=supf∈𝒮bβf​(τ).B(\tau)=\sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{S}}\beta_{f}(\tau)\,\,\textup{and}\,\,B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{b}}\beta_{f}(\tau).

Because of its important relation to the fine properties of harmonic measures in the complex plane, see [45], the universal integral means spectra of univalent functions have been studied extensively in recent years. It is an important and difficult problem to find out the exact values of the universal integral means spectra B⁡(τ)B(\tau) and Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau). We shall first review some main known results and open problems for real τ\tau in this topic. It was first observed by Makarov in [45] that

Theorem 1.2.

B⁡(τ)=max⁡{Bb​(τ),3​τ−1},τ∈ℝ.B(\tau)=\max\{B_{b}(\tau),3\tau-1\},\,\tau\in\mathbb{R}.

For large τ\tau, Feng and MacGregor proved in [24] that B⁡(τ)=3​τ−1,τ≥25.B(\tau)=3\tau-1,\,\,\tau\geq\frac{2}{5}. Also for large τ\tau, see [50], we have Bb​(τ)=τ−1,τ≥2.B_{b}(\tau)=\tau-1,\,\,\tau\geq 2. By considering the lacunary series, Kayumov showed in [41] that B⁡(τ)>τ25,  0<τ≤25.B(\tau)>\frac{\tau^{2}}{5},\,\,0<\tau\leq\frac{2}{5}. In the paper [18], after establishing an important result in the theory of harmonic measures, Carleson and Makarov obtained that

Theorem 1.3.

There is a constant τ∗<0\tau_{*}<0 such that Bb​(τ)=B⁡(τ)=|τ|−1,τ≤τ∗.B_{b}(\tau)=B(\tau)=|\tau|-1,\,\,\tau\leq\tau_{*}.

It is only known that τ∗≤−2\tau_{*}\leq-2. It is conjectured that τ∗=−2\tau_{*}=-2. This is equivalent to the celebrated Brennan conjecture that B⁡(−2)=Bb​(−2)=1B(-2)=B_{b}(-2)=1, which was raised in [16]. There have been many studies on the Brennan conjecture, see for example, [14], [15], [8], [29], [30], [33], [54], [56]. The current best upper bound estimate about B⁡(−2)B(-2) is provided by Hedenmalm and Shimorin in [33]. In the paper [17], Carleson and Jones conjectured that Bb​(1)=14B_{b}(1)=\frac{1}{4}. A more generalized conjecture was given by Kraetzer in [42] that

Conjecture 1.4.

Let τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R}. Then

Bb​(τ)={τ24,if​τ∈[−2,2],|τ|−1,if​τ∈(−∞,−2)∪(2,+∞).B_{b}(\tau)=\begin{cases}\frac{\tau^{2}}{4},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\,\tau\in[-2,2],\\ |\tau|-1,\;\text{if}\;\,\tau\in(-\infty,-2)\cup(2,+\infty).\end{cases}

For the complex exponents τ\tau, there are only several known results about B⁡(τ)B(\tau) and Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau). In an unpublished preprint [12], Binder extended Makarov’s Theorem 1.2 to the complex setting.

Theorem 1.5.

(1) If Re​(τ)>0\textup{Re}(\tau)>0, then B⁡(τ)=max⁡{Bb​(τ),|τ|+2​Re​(τ)−1}.B(\tau)=\max\{B_{b}(\tau),|\tau|+2\textup{Re}(\tau)-1\}.

(2) If Re​(τ)≤0\textup{Re}({\tau})\leq 0, then B​(τ)=Bb​(τ)B(\tau)=B_{b}(\tau).

In a 1987 paper [10], Becker and Pommerenke extended the Brennan conjecture to the complex case, asking whether Bb​(τ)=1B_{b}(\tau)=1 whenever |τ|=2|\tau|=2. Baranov and Hedenmalm proved in [7] that

Theorem 1.6.
Bb​(2−τ)≤1−Re​(τ)+[9​e22+o⁡(1)]​|τ|2​log⁡1|τ|,as​|τ|→0.B_{b}(2-\tau)\leq 1-\textup{Re}(\tau)+[\frac{9e^{2}}{2}+o(1)]|\tau|^{2}\log\frac{1}{|\tau|},\,\,\,\textup{as}\,\,\,|\tau|\rightarrow 0.

Binder continued to study the integral means spectrum in [13] for complex exponents and proved the following

Theorem 1.7.

For each θ∈(−π,π]\theta\in(-\pi,\pi], there exists Tθ>0T_{\theta}>0 such that Bb​(t​ei​θ)=t−1B_{b}(te^{i\theta})=t-1 for t≥Tθt\geq T_{\theta}.

Also in [13], Binder conjectured that the following generalization of Kraetzer’s conjecture still holds.

Conjecture 1.8.

Let τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}. Then

Bb​(τ)={τ24,if​|τ|<2,|τ|−1,if​|τ|≥2.B_{b}(\tau)=\begin{cases}\frac{\tau^{2}}{4},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\text{if}\;\,|\tau|<2,\\ |\tau|-1,\;\text{if}\;\,|\tau|\geq 2.\end{cases}

More known results on the universal integral means spectrum and related topics can be found in the monograph [27, Chapter VIII] and recent survey [32] given by Hedenmalm and Sola.

From the fractal approximation principle(see [45] and [17]), we have

Theorem 1.9.

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, we have Bb​(τ)=supf∈𝒮qβf​(τ).B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}}\beta_{f}(\tau).

Remark 1.10.

Here, 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} is the class of all univalent functions ff that belong to 𝒮b\mathcal{S}_{b} and admit a quasiconformal extension to ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}}. In the rest of the paper, when a univalent function ff belongs to 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}, we will still use ff to denote its quasiconformal extension.

There have been some studies on the integral means spectra of univalent functions admitting a quasiconformal extension, see for example [34], [35], [36], [37], [38], [51] and [52]. From Theorem 1.9, we can see the problem that determining the exact values of Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau) as a global extremal problem in the class 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}. To enrich the understanding of the theory of integral means spectra of univalent functions, in the present paper, we continue to consider the following problem, which differs from previous studies that finding a better estimation for Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau).

Problem 1.11.

(1) For fixed τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C} with τ≠0\tau\neq 0, what topology can be endowed upon the class 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} such that the integral means spectrum βf​(τ)\beta_{f}(\tau) is continuous on 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}? (2) For given τ≠0\tau\neq 0, does there exist at least one extremal function for Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau)? (3) If the extremal functions for Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau) exist, in which subset of 𝒮\mathcal{S} do they lie?

Here and later, we say a function f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S} is an extremal function for Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau) if βf​(τ)=Bb​(τ)\beta_{f}(\tau)=B_{b}(\tau). In the recent work [39], we have studied Problem 1.11 for real τ\tau. It has been pointed out that the functional I:f→βf​(τ),f∈𝒮qI:f\rightarrow\beta_{f}(\tau),f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}, is not continuous on 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} under the locally uniformly convergence topology, see [39, Remark 5.8]. In [39], we introduced and studied the integral means spectrum (IMS) functionals on the Teichmüller spaces. It has been proved in [39] that all IMS functionals on the universal Teichmüller space, the closure of the universal Teichmüller curve, and the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space are continuous. It was also shown in [39] that the real exponential integral means spectrum of any univalent function admitting a quasiconformal extension to ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}} is strictly less than the universal integral means spectrum. This result means that, for τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R} with τ≠0\tau\neq 0, the extremal functions for Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau) cannot be from the class 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}. The first main purpose of this paper is to extend these results to the complex setting. We shall prove that

Theorem 1.12.

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, the IMS functional IT:[μ]T↦βfμ​(τ),[μ]T∈T,I_{{T}}:[\mu]_{T}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau),\,\,[\mu]_{T}\in{T}, is continuous.

Theorem 1.13.

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, the IMS functional IA​T:[μ]A​T↦βfμ​(τ),[μ]A​T∈A​T,I_{{AT}}:[\mu]_{AT}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau),\,\,[\mu]_{AT}\in{AT}, is continuous.

Theorem 1.14.

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, the IMS functional I𝒯¯:ϕ↦βfϕ​(τ),ϕ∈𝒯¯,I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau),\,\,\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}, is continuous.

Theorem 1.15.

Let τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C} with τ≠0\tau\neq 0. Then we have βf​(τ)<Bb​(τ)\beta_{f}(\tau)<B_{b}(\tau) for any f∈𝒮qf\in\mathcal{S}_{q}.

The rest of paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we will fix some notations used in this paper and recall some basic properties about univalent functions, quasiconformal mappings, and the definitions of quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces. Also, Theorem 1.12-1.15 will be restated in Section 2. We will provide some lemmas in Section 3. We shall give the proof of Theorem 1.12 and 1.13 in Section 4. We will prove Theorem 1.14 and 1.15 in Section 5. In Section 6, we study the integral means spectra of univalent rational functions in Δ\Delta and prove that the Brennan conjecture is true for this class of functions. We also check that the Brennan conjecture holds for any univalent function from the unit disk onto the interior of a bounded polygon. In Section 7, for IMS functionals on Teichmüller spaces, univalent rational functions, and a multiplication operator whose norm is closely related to the Brennan conjecture, we finally present some remarks and raise some problems and conjectures.

2. Preliminaries and restatement of the first main results

In this section, we first fix some notations that will be used later, and then recall some basic definitions and properties of univalent functions(conformal mappings), quasiconformal mappings, and quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces. For the main references, see [20, 47, 43, 44] and [5, 25, 21, 23, 22, 43, 58].

We let Δ∗=ℂ^−Δ¯\Delta^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\Delta} be the exterior of Δ\Delta and let 𝕋=∂Δ=∂Δ∗\mathbb{T}=\partial\Delta=\partial\Delta^{*} to be the unit circle. We let 𝒜⁡(Δ)\mathcal{A}(\Delta) denote the class of all analytic functions in Δ\Delta. We use the notation Δ⁡(r)\Delta(r) to denote the disk centered at 00 with radius rr. For two compact sets X,YX,Y of the complex plane, we define the distance of XX and YY, denoted by dist​{X,Y}{\text{dist}}\{X,Y\}, as dist​{X,Y}:=minx∈X,y∈Y⁡|x−y|.{\textup{dist}}\{X,Y\}:=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}|x-y|. Let Ω\Omega be a simply connected proper subdomain of ℂ\mathbb{C}. We shall use ρΩ\rho_{\Omega} to denote the hyperbolic metric with curvature −4-4 in Ω\Omega. That is ρΩ​(w)=|g′​(w)|/(1−|g⁡(w)|2),w∈Ω.\rho_{\Omega}(w)=|g^{\prime}(w)|/({1-|g(w)|^{2}}),\,\,w\in\Omega. Here gg is a univalent function from Ω\Omega to Δ\Delta. In particular, ρΔ​(z)=(1−|z|2)−1,z∈Δ.\rho_{\Delta}(z)=(1-|z|^{2})^{-1},z\in\Delta.

2.1. Univalent functions and quasiconformal mappings

It is well known that

Proposition 2.1.

Let f∈𝒰f\in\mathcal{U}. Then, for any z∈Δz\in\Delta,

dist​(f⁡(z),∂f⁡(Δ))≤(1−|z|2)|f′​(z)|≤4​dist​(f⁡(z),∂f⁡(Δ)).{\textup{dist}}(f(z),\partial f(\Delta))\leq(1-|z|^{2})|f^{\prime}(z)|\leq 4{\textup{dist}}(f(z),\partial f(\Delta)).

We let Ej{E}_{j} be the Banach space of functions ϕ∈𝒜⁡(Δ)\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta) with the norm

∥ϕ∥Ej:=supz∈Δ|ϕ(z)|(1−|z|2)j<∞,j=1,2.\|\phi\|_{E_{j}}:=\sup_{z\in\Delta}|\phi(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{j}<\infty,\,\,\,\,j=1,2.

Nf​(z):=f′′​(z)f′​(z),z∈Ω,N_{f}(z):=\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(z)}{{f^{\prime}(z)}},\,z\in\Omega,

Sf​(z):=[Nf​(z)]′−12​[Nf​(z)]2=f′′′​(z)f′​(z)−32​[f′′​(z)f′​(z)]2,z∈Ω.S_{f}(z):=[N_{f}(z)]^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2}[N_{f}(z)]^{2}=\frac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(z)}{f^{\prime}(z)}-\frac{3}{2}\left[\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(z)}{f^{\prime}(z)}\right]^{2},\,z\in\Omega.

Let gg be another locally univalent function in f⁡(Ω)f(\Omega). Then we have

(2.1) Ng∘f​(z)=Ng​(f⁡(z))​[f′​(z)]+Nf​(z),z∈Ω,N_{g\circ f}(z)=N_{g}(f(z))[f^{\prime}(z)]+N_{f}(z),\,\,z\in\Omega,

It is well known that

|Nf​(z)|​(1−|z|2)≤6​and​|Sf​(z)|​(1−|z|2)2≤6,|N_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})\leq 6\,\,{\text{and}}\,\,|S_{f}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{2}\leq 6,

𝐍={ϕ∈𝒜(Δ):ϕ=Nf(z),f∈𝒮},\mathbf{N}=\{\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\,\phi=N_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}\},

𝐒={ϕ∈𝒜(Δ):ϕ=Sf(z),f∈𝒮}.\mathbf{S}=\{\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\,\phi=S_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}\}.

Then 𝐍⊂E1\mathbf{N}\subset E_{1} and 𝐒⊂E2\mathbf{S}\subset E_{2}. Moreover, we have

Proposition 2.2.

𝐍\mathbf{N} and 𝐒\mathbf{S} are closed in E1E_{1} and E2E_{2}, respectively.

‖μf‖∞=ess supz∈Ω⁡|μf​(z)|<1.\|\mu_{f}\|_{\infty}=\mathop{\text{ess sup}}\limits_{z\in\Omega}|\mu_{f}(z)|<1.

∂¯​f=fz¯:=12​(∂∂x+i​∂∂y)​f,\bar{\partial}f=f_{\bar{z}}:=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)f,

(2.3) μg∘f−1∘f⁡(z)=1χ​μg​(z)−μf​(z)1−μf​(z)¯​μg​(z),χ=∂f¯∂f,z∈Ω1.\mu_{g\circ f^{-1}}\circ f(z)=\frac{1}{\chi}\frac{\mu_{g}(z)-\mu_{f}(z)}{1-\overline{\mu_{f}(z)}\mu_{g}(z)},\,\,\chi=\frac{\overline{\partial f}}{\partial f},\,\,\,z\in\Omega_{1}.

Let ff be a bounded univalent function in a Jordan domain Ω\Omega of ℂ\mathbb{C} admitting a quasiconformal extension (still denoted by ff) to ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}}. The boundary dilatation of ff, denoted by b⁡(f)b(f), is defined as

(2.4) b⁡(f):=inf{‖μf|Ω∗−E‖∞:E​ is a compact set in​Ω∗}.b(f):=\inf\{\|\mu_{f}|_{\Omega^{*}-E}\|_{\infty}:\,E{\text{ is a compact set in}}\,\,\Omega^{*}\}.

2.2. Quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded Jordan domain in ℂ\mathbb{C} with 0∈Ω0\in\Omega, and let Ω∗=ℂ^−Ω¯\Omega^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\Omega}. We use M⁡(Ω∗)M(\Omega^{*}) to denote the open unit ball of the Banach space L∞​(Ω∗)L^{\infty}({\Omega}^{*}) of essentially bounded measurable functions in Ω∗{\Omega}^{*}. For μ∈M⁡(Ω∗)\mu\in M({\Omega}^{*}), let fμf_{\mu} be the quasiconformal mapping in the extended complex plane ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}} with complex dilatation equal to μ\mu in Ω∗\Omega^{*}, equal to 00 in Ω\Omega, normalized fμ​(0)=0,fμ′​(0)=1,fμ​(∞)=∞f_{\mu}(0)=0,\,f^{\prime}_{\mu}(0)=1,\,f_{\mu}(\infty)=\infty. We say two elements μ\mu and ν\nu in M⁡(Ω∗)M(\Omega^{*}) are equivalent, denoted by μ∼ν\mu\sim\nu, if fμ|Ω=fν|Ωf_{\mu}|_{\Omega}=f_{\nu}|_{\Omega}. The equivalence class of μ\mu is denoted by [μ]T⁡(Ω)[\mu]_{T(\Omega)}. Then T(Ω)=M(Ω∗)/∼T(\Omega)=M(\Omega^{*})/\sim is one model of Teichmüller space of the domain Ω\Omega.

For any μ,ν∈M⁡(Ω∗)\mu,\nu\in M(\Omega^{*}), we let

σ⁡(μ,ν)​(ζ):=μ⁡(ζ)−ν⁡(ζ)1−ν⁡(ζ)¯​μ​(ζ),ζ∈Ω∗.\sigma(\mu,\nu)(\zeta):=\frac{\mu(\zeta)-\nu(\zeta)}{1-{\overline{\nu(\zeta)}}\mu(\zeta)},\,\zeta\in\Omega^{*}.

The (hyperbolic) distance dΩ​(μ,ν)d_{\Omega}(\mu,\nu) of two elements μ,ν\mu,\nu in M⁡(Ω∗)M(\Omega^{*}) is defined as

dΩ​(μ,ν):=12​log⁡1+‖σ⁡(μ,ν)‖∞1−‖σ⁡(μ,ν)‖∞=tanh−1⁡‖σ⁡(μ,ν)‖∞.d_{\Omega}(\mu,\nu):=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+\|\sigma(\mu,\nu)\|_{\infty}}{1-\|\sigma(\mu,\nu)\|_{\infty}}=\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu,\nu)\|_{\infty}.

The Teichmüller distance dT​([μ]T⁡(Ω),[ν]T⁡(Ω))d_{T}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)}) of two points [μ]T⁡(Ω)[\mu]_{T(\Omega)}, [ν]T⁡(Ω)[\nu]_{T(\Omega)} in T⁡(Ω)T(\Omega) is defined as

dT​([μ]T⁡(Ω),[ν]T⁡(Ω))\displaystyle d_{T}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)},[\nu]_{T(\Omega)}) =\displaystyle= infμ1∼μ,ν1∼ν{tanh−1⁡‖σ⁡(μ1,ν1)‖∞}\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\sim\mu,\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}\Big\}
=\displaystyle= infμ1∼μ,ν1∼ν{12​log⁡1+‖σ⁡(μ1,ν1)‖∞1−‖σ⁡(μ1,ν1)‖∞}.\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\sim\mu,\nu_{1}\sim\nu}\Big\{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}}{1-\|\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\|_{\infty}}\Big\}.

We say μ\mu and ν\nu in M⁡(Ω∗)M({\Omega}^{*}) are asymptotically equivalent, denoted by μ≈ν\mu\approx\nu, if there exists ν~\widetilde{\nu} in M⁡(Ω∗){M}(\Omega^{*}) such that [ν~]T⁡(Ω)=[ν]T⁡(Ω)[\widetilde{\nu}]_{T(\Omega)}=[{\nu}]_{T(\Omega)} and ν~​(ζ)−μ​(ζ)→0\widetilde{\nu}(\zeta)-{\mu}(\zeta)\rightarrow 0 as dist​(ζ,∂Ω)→0+\textup{dist}(\zeta,\partial\Omega)\rightarrow 0^{+}. The asymptotic equivalence of μ\mu will be denoted by [μ]A​T​(Ω)[\mu]_{AT(\Omega)}. The asymptotic Teichmüller space A​T​(Ω)AT(\Omega) is the set of all asymptotic equivalence classes [μ]A​T​(Ω)[\mu]_{AT(\Omega)} of elements μ\mu in M⁡(Ω∗)M({\Omega}^{*}). The Teichmüller distance dA​T​([μ]A​T​(Ω),[ν]A​T​(Ω))d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)}) of two points [μ]A​T​(Ω)[\mu]_{AT(\Omega)}, [ν]A​T​(Ω)[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)} in A​T​(Ω)AT(\Omega) is defined as

dA​T​([μ]A​T​(Ω),[ν]A​T​(Ω))\displaystyle d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)},[\nu]_{AT(\Omega)}) =\displaystyle= infμ1≈μ,ν1≈ν{tanh−1h∗(σ(μ1,ν1)}\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu,\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\tanh^{-1}h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1})\Big\}
=\displaystyle= infμ1≈μ,ν1≈ν{12​log⁡1+h∗​(σ⁡(μ1,ν1))1−h∗​(σ⁡(μ1,ν1))}.\displaystyle\inf\limits_{\mu_{1}\approx\mu,\nu_{1}\approx\nu}\Big\{\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))}{1-h^{*}(\sigma(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}))}\Big\}.

Here, for μ∈M⁡(Ω∗)\mu\in M(\Omega^{*}), h∗​(μ)h^{*}(\mu) is defined as

(2.5) h∗​(μ)=inf{‖μ|Ω∗−E‖∞:E​ is a compact set in​Ω∗}.h^{*}(\mu)=\inf\{\|\mu|_{\Omega^{*}-E}\|_{\infty}:\,E{\text{ is a compact set in}}\,\,\Omega^{*}\}.

We note that h∗​(μ)=b⁡(fμ)h^{*}(\mu)=b(f_{\mu}) for μ∈M⁡(Ω∗)\mu\in M(\Omega^{*}), here b⁡(fμ)b(f_{\mu}) is defined as in (2.4).

Remark 2.4.

We shall mainly consider the Teichmüller spaces defined on Δ\Delta. We next will use TT, A​TAT to denote T⁡(Δ)T(\Delta), A​T​(Δ)AT(\Delta), respectively. TT and A​TAT are known as universal Teichmüller space and universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, respectively. For the sake of simplicity, the equivalence classes [μ]T⁡(Δ)[\mu]_{T(\Delta)} and [μ]A​T​(Δ)[\mu]_{AT(\Delta)} will be denoted by [μ]T[\mu]_{T} and [μ]A​T[\mu]_{AT}, respectively.

Remark 2.5.

Note that for any f∈𝒮qf\in\mathcal{S}_{q}, we can find a μ∈M⁡(Δ∗)\mu\in M(\Delta^{*}) such that f=σ∘fμf=\sigma\circ f_{\mu}, σ\sigma is a Möbius transformation. Then we check from Theorem 1.9 that

Bb​(τ)=sup[μ]T∈Tβfμ​(τ)B_{b}(\tau)=\sup\limits_{{[\mu]_{T}}\in T}\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau)

for each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}.

2.3. Restatement of the first main results

We will study the following IMS functional defined on TT and prove that

Theorem 2.6 (=Theorem 1).

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, the IMS functional IT:[μ]T↦βfμ​(τ)I_{{T}}:[\mu]_{T}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau) on TT is continuous.

For the IMS functional on the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, we shall show that

Theorem 2.7 (=Theorem 2).

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, the IMS functional IA​T:[μ]A​T↦βfμ​(τ)I_{{AT}}:[\mu]_{AT}\mapsto\beta_{f_{\mu}}(\tau) is well-defined and continuous on A​TAT.

We set

𝒯:={ϕ:ϕ=Nf(z),f∈𝒮q}.\mathcal{T}:=\{\phi:\phi=N_{f}(z),f\in\mathcal{S}_{q}\}.

𝒯\mathcal{T} is seen as one model of universal Teichmüller curve, see [11, 55]. It is known that 𝒯\mathcal{T} is an open connected subset of E1E_{1}, see [58]. Since 𝐍\mathbf{N} is closed in E1E_{1}, then the closure 𝒯¯\overline{\mathcal{T}} of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is contained in 𝐍\mathbf{N}. We view 𝒯¯\overline{\mathcal{T}} as a model for the closure of the universal Teichmüller curve. For any ϕ∈𝒯¯\phi\in\overline{\mathcal{T}}, there is a unique univalent function fϕ​(z)f_{\phi}(z) with fϕ∈𝒮f_{\phi}\in\mathcal{S} and such that ϕ​(z)=Nfϕ​(z).\phi(z)=N_{f_{\phi}}(z). Actually, we can take

(2.6) fϕ​(z)=∫0ze∫0ζϕ⁡(w)​𝑑w​𝑑ζ,z∈Δ.f_{\phi}(z)=\int_{0}^{z}e^{\int_{0}^{\zeta}\phi(w)dw}d\zeta,\,\,\,z\in\Delta.

We shall prove that

Theorem 2.8 (=Theorem 3).

For each τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C}, the IMS functional I𝒯¯:ϕ↦βfϕ​(τ)I_{\overline{\mathcal{T}}}:\phi\mapsto\beta_{f_{\phi}}(\tau) is continuous on 𝒯¯\overline{\mathcal{T}}.

Also, we will prove the following result, which indicates that the IMS functional on the class 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q} satisfies the maximum modulus principle.

Theorem 2.9 (=Theorem 4).

Let τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb{C} with τ≠0\tau\neq 0. Then we have βf​(τ)<Bb​(τ)\beta_{f}(\tau)<B_{b}(\tau) for any f∈𝒮qf\in\mathcal{S}_{q}.

4. Proof of Theorem 1.12 and 1.13

Note that dA​T​([μ]A​T,[ν]A​T)≤dT​([μ]T,[ν]T)d_{AT}([\mu]_{AT},[\nu]_{AT})\leq d_{T}([\mu]_{T},[\nu]_{T}) for any μ,ν∈M⁡(Δ∗)\mu,\nu\in M(\Delta^{*}), we see that the statement that IA​TI_{AT} is continuous on A​TAT implies Theorem 1.12. Hence we only need to prove Theorem 1.13. By studying the Pre-Schwarzian derivative model of the universal asymptotic Teichmüller space, we have proved in [39] that Theorem 1.13 holds for real τ\tau. We will use a more direct way to show that Theorem 1.13 holds for all complex numbers τ\tau. More precisely, we will prove Theorem 1.13 by using some arguments from the theory of Teichmüller spaces and some results from the extremal theory of quasiconformal mappings.

4.1. Isomorphism mapping between Teichmüller spaces

We first recall some arguments from the theory of quasiconformal Teichmüller spaces. For a fixed ω∈M⁡(Δ∗)\omega\in M(\Delta^{*}), let 𝛀:=fω​(Δ)\mathbf{\Omega}:=f_{\omega}(\Delta) and 𝛀∗=ℂ^−𝛀¯\mathbf{\Omega}^{*}=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}-\overline{\mathbf{\Omega}}. 4.2. Extremal theory of quasiconformal mappings

We recall some definitions and results on the extremal theory of quasiconformal mappings. For a bounded Jordan domain Ω\Omega in ℂ\mathbb{C} with 0∈Ω0\in\Omega, let μ∈M⁡(Ω)\mu\in M(\Omega). We define

k0​([μ]T⁡(Ω))=inf{‖ν‖∞:ν∼μ},k_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})=\inf\{\|\nu\|_{\infty}:\nu\sim\mu\},

h0​([μ]T⁡(Ω))=inf{h∗​(ν):ν∼μ}.h_{0}([\mu]_{T(\Omega)})=\inf\{h^{*}(\nu):{\nu}\sim\mu\}.

H0​([μ]A​T​(Ω))=inf{h∗​(ν):ν≈μ}.H_{0}([\mu]_{AT(\Omega)})=\inf\{h^{*}(\nu):{\nu}\approx\mu\}.

6. Integral means spectra of the univalent rational functions

In this section, we study the integral means spectra of univalent rational functions in the unit disk Δ\Delta. Since directly studying the integral means spectrum of univalent rational functions in Δ\Delta is inconvenient, we enlarge the scope to the general class of locally univalent functions in Δ\Delta. The locally univalent functions allow for the definition of a generalized integral means spectrum, see (6.11) below. In particular, this generalized spectrum coincides with the classical one for the univalent rational functions. We then completely determine the generalized integral means spectra for a certain class of locally functions, thereby proving that univalent rational functions in the unit disk satisfy the Brennan conjecture. We also check that the Brennan conjecture is true for any univalent function from the unit disk onto the interior of a bounded polygon.

In the rest of the paper, the notation Pn​(z)P_{n}(z) denotes a polynomial of degree nn, n∈ℕ∪{0}n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}. In particular, PnP_{n} is a complex constant when n=0n=0. We denote by ℛ\mathcal{R} the class of all rational functions RR in Δ\Delta with R⁡(0)=R′​(0)−1=0R(0)=R^{\prime}(0)-1=0 and which have no poles in Δ\Delta. Let Ω\Omega be a subset of the complex plane. If RR is analytic in Ω\Omega, we say RR has no zeros, or one zero in Ω\Omega if the equation R⁡(z)=0R(z)=0 has no roots, or one root in Ω\Omega, respectively. If RR is analytic in Ω∖Ω1\Omega\setminus\Omega_{1}, Ω1\Omega_{1} is a finite (or empty) subset of Ω\Omega, we will say RR has no critical points, or one critical point in Ω\Omega, if there is no point z∈Ωz\in\Omega, or one point z∈Ωz\in\Omega such that RR is analytic in zz and R′​(z)=0R^{\prime}(z)=0, respectively. A rational function R∈ℛR\in\mathcal{R} can be uniquely represented as

R⁡(z)=Pn​(z)Pm​(z)=z+a2​z2+⋯+an​zn1+b1​z+⋯+bm​zm.R(z)=\frac{P_{n}(z)}{P_{m}(z)}=\frac{z+a_{2}z^{2}+\cdots+a_{n}z^{n}}{1+b_{1}z+\cdots+b_{m}z^{m}}.

Here, PnP_{n} and PmP_{m} have no common factors except 1 and Pm​(z)P_{m}(z) has no zeros in Δ\Delta.

6.1. Certain locally univalent functions and the main result of this section

We use 𝒰R\mathcal{U}_{R} to denote the class of all univalent rational functions RR belonging to ℛ\mathcal{R}. We denote by 𝒰P\mathcal{U}_{P} the class which consists of all univalent polynomials contained in 𝒰R\mathcal{U}_{R}. It is easy to see that 𝒰P\mathcal{U}_{P} is contained in 𝒮b\mathcal{S}_{b}. It should be pointed out that the univalent polynomials are dense in 𝒮\mathcal{S}, see [20] or [2]. This fact is one of the reasons for our investigation of the classes 𝒰P\mathcal{U}_{P} and 𝒰R\mathcal{U}_{R}. When R⁡(z)R(z) belongs to 𝒰R\mathcal{U}_{R}, we know from the Koebe distortion theorem that

|R⁡(z)|≤|z|(1−|z|)2.|R(z)|\leq\frac{|z|}{(1-|z|)^{2}}.

In view of this fact, we shall consider the following three classes of rational functions contained in ℛ\mathcal{R}.

As we shall see later, the integral means spectra of functions R∈𝒰RR\in\mathcal{U}_{R} that have no critical points on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, are different from those of functions RR that have at least one critical point on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Take P1​(z)=zP_{1}(z)=z, then P1′​(z)=1P^{\prime}_{1}(z)=1 so that P1P_{1} has no critical points on 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

We now present the main result of this section.

Theorem 6.20.

Let τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R} and let R∈(𝒬I∪𝒬I​I∪𝒬I​I​I)R\in({\mathcal{Q}_{I}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{II}}\cup{\mathcal{Q}_{III}}). Then

(𝐛𝟏)({\bf b_{1}}) if RR has no critical points on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, then β~R​(τ)=0{\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0,

β~R​(τ)={0,for​τ∈(−1,0),|τ|−1,for​τ≤−1,{\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=\begin{cases}0,\;\;\;\quad\,\,\,\,\text{for}\,\;\tau\in(-1,0),\\ |\tau|-1,\;\text{for}\,\;\tau\leq-1,\end{cases}

(𝐂)(\bf C) when τ>0\tau>0, we have

(𝐜𝟏)({\bf c_{1}}) if RR belongs to the class 𝒬I\mathcal{Q}_{I}, then β~R​(τ)=0{\widetilde{\beta}}_{R}(\tau)=0,

(𝐜𝟐)({\bf c_{2}}) if RR belongs to the class 𝒬I​I\mathcal{Q}_{II}, then

Remark 6.27.

We recall the Schwarz-Christoffel formula for the unit disk, see [1, Page 236]. Let ff be a univalent function (conformal map) from the unit disk Δ\Delta onto the interior of a bounded polygon 𝒫\mathcal{P} with vertices z1,…,zn,n≥3z_{1},\dots,z_{n},n\geq 3, and corresponding interior angles α1​π,…,αn​π\alpha_{1}\pi,\dots,\alpha_{n}\pi. Then the derivative of ff is given by

f′​(z)=C​∏k=1n(z−ak)αk−1,z∈Δ,f^{\prime}(z)=C\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(z-{a_{k}}\right)^{\alpha_{k}-1},\quad z\in\Delta,

where a1,a2,…,ana_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n} are points on the unit circle 𝕋\mathbb{T} and CC is a non-zero complex constant.

Note that for r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1),

When Pn∈𝒰PP_{n}\in\mathcal{U}_{P} has no critical points on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, we have pointed out that NPnN_{P_{n}} belongs to E1,0{E_{1,0}}. If Conjecture 7.10 holds, namely, Bb​(τ)B_{b}(\tau) has an extremal function ff whose Pre-Schwarzian derivative lies on ∂𝒯\partial\mathcal{T}, then, by using the same arguments as in Remark 7.22, we can obtain that [Nf]E1[N_{f}]_{E_{1}} lies on the boundary of 𝐍~q\widetilde{\mathbf{N}}_{q}. 7.4. The final part of remarks

In the paper [54], Shimorin introduced and studied the following multiplication operator ℳf\mathcal{M}_{f}, induced by the Schwarzian derivative of univalent function f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S},

ℳf​(ϕ)​(z):=Sf​(z)​ϕ​(z),ϕ∈𝒜⁡(Δ).\mathcal{M}_{f}(\phi)(z):=S_{f}(z)\phi(z),\,\phi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta).

There is a close connection between the norm of multiplication operator ℳf\mathcal{M}_{f} and the Brennan conjecture. It has been proved in [54] that

Proposition 7.26.

If some univalent function f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S} satisfies that

(7.4) ‖ℳf‖2≤36​(α+3)​(α+5)(α+2)​(α+4),\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|^{2}\leq\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)},

for any α>0\alpha>0. Then βf​(−2)≤1\beta_{f}(-2)\leq 1, that is to say, the Brennan conjecture is true for the function ff. Here,

‖ℳf‖=sup‖ϕ‖α≠0,ϕ∈ℋα2​(Δ)‖Sf​(z)​ϕ​(z)‖α+4‖ϕ⁡(z)‖α:=𝕄f​(α).\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}\neq 0,\phi\in\mathcal{H}_{\alpha}^{2}(\Delta)}\frac{\|S_{f}(z)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}}{\|\phi(z)\|_{\alpha}}:=\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha).
Remark 7.27.

It is easy to see that, if for any α>0\alpha>0, (7.4) holds for all f∈𝒮qf\in\mathcal{S}_{q}, then the Brennan conjecture is true. On the other hand, it has been pointed out in [54, Page 1633] that there exists univalent function f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S} such that 𝕄f​(α)>𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)>\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha) when α>−1\alpha>-1. Meanwhile, for any α>−1\alpha>-1, it has been shown in [54] that,

(7.5) 𝕄κΘ2​(α)=36​(α+3)​(α+5)(α+2)​(α+4).\mathbb{M}_{\kappa_{\Theta}}^{2}(\alpha)=\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.

Here, κΘ\kappa_{\Theta} are the Koebe function κ\kappa and its rotations, which are defined as

(7.6) κΘ(z):=z(1−ei​Θ​z)2,Θ∈(−π,π],z∈Δ.\kappa_{\Theta}(z):=\frac{z}{(1-e^{i\Theta}z)^{2}},\,\Theta\in(-\pi,\pi],\,z\in\Delta.

Let ϱ\varrho be a Möbius transformation. We conclude that ϱ∘κΘ∈𝒮\varrho\circ\kappa_{\Theta}\in\mathcal{S}, if and only if ϱ\varrho has the form as

ϱ⁡(ζ):=ϱc​(ζ)=ζ1+c​ei​Θ​ζ,0≤c≤4.\varrho(\zeta):=\varrho_{c}(\zeta)=\frac{\zeta}{1+ce^{i\Theta}\zeta},0\leq c\leq 4.

Because the Koebe function and its rotations are the unique class of extremal functions in 𝒮\mathcal{S} for some extremal problems in the theory of univalent functions, thus, it is natural to guess that the functions ϱc∘κΘ\varrho_{c}\circ\kappa_{\Theta}, (c,Θ)∈[0,4]×(−π,π](c,\Theta)\in[0,4]\times(-\pi,\pi], may be the unique class that induce the biggest norm of the operator ℳf\mathcal{M}_{f} in the class 𝒮\mathcal{S} for any α>0\alpha>0. ≥36​Γ⁡(α+6)24​[Γ⁡(λ+2)]2⋅[Γ⁡(λ)]2Γ⁡(α+2)=9​(α+2)​(α+3)​(α+4)​(α+5)4​[λ⁡(λ+1)]2.\displaystyle\geq 36\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+6)}{2^{4}[\Gamma(\lambda+2)]^{2}}\cdot\frac{[\Gamma(\lambda)]^{2}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}=\frac{9(\alpha+2)(\alpha+3)(\alpha+4)(\alpha+5)}{4[\lambda(\lambda+1)]^{2}}.

Let λ→(α2+1)+\lambda\rightarrow{(\frac{\alpha}{2}+1)}^{+}, we obtain that

𝕄P32​(α)≥36​(α+3)​(α+5)(α+2)​(α+4).\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}^{2}(\alpha)\geq\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.

This finishes the proof of Proposition 7.28. ∎

We continue to investigate the properties of ‖ℳf‖\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|. Let α>−1\alpha>-1, we define the functional Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} as

Λα:Sf↦‖ℳf‖=𝕄f​(α),f∈𝒮.\Lambda_{\alpha}:S_{f}\mapsto\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|=\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha),\,\,f\in\mathcal{S}.

We obtain that

Proposition 7.29.

For any fixed α>−1\alpha>-1, Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} is continuous on 𝐒¯\overline{\mathbf{S}}, the closure of 𝐒{\mathbf{S}}.

Proof.

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be small. For f1,f2∈𝒮f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathcal{S} with Sf1,Sf2∈𝐒¯S_{f_{1}},S_{f_{2}}\in\overline{\mathbf{S}}, we assume that ‖Sf1−Sf2‖E2=ε\|S_{f_{1}}-S_{f_{2}}\|_{E_{2}}=\varepsilon so that

|Sf1​(z)−Sf2​(z)|​(1−|z|2)2≤ε,|S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)|(1-|z|^{2})^{2}\leq\varepsilon,

for all z∈Δz\in\Delta. Then,

𝕄f12​(α)=sup‖ϕ‖α=1‖Sf1​(z)​ϕ​(z)‖α+42\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{f_{1}}^{2}(\alpha)=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\|S_{f_{1}}(z)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}
=sup‖ϕ‖α=1‖[Sf1​(z)−Sf2​(z)+Sf2​(z)]​ϕ​(z)‖α+42\displaystyle=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\|[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)+S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}
≤sup‖ϕ‖α=1‖|[Sf1​(z)−Sf2​(z)]​ϕ​(z)|+|Sf2​(z)​ϕ​(z)|‖α+42\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\||[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)|+|S_{f_{2}}(z)\phi(z)|\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}
=sup‖ϕ‖α=1‖[Sf1​(z)−Sf2​(z)]​ϕ​(z)‖α+42+‖Sf2​(z)​ϕ​(z)‖α+42\displaystyle=\sup_{\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1}\|[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}+\|S_{f_{2}}(z)\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}
+(α+5)∬Δ2|Sf1(z)−Sf2(z)||Sf2(z)||ϕ(z)|2(1−|z|2)α+4d​x​d​yπ.\displaystyle\quad\qquad\qquad+(\alpha+5)\iint_{\Delta}2|S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)||S_{f_{2}}(z)||\phi(z)|^{2}(1-|z|^{2})^{\alpha+4}\frac{dxdy}{\pi}.

Note that, for ‖ϕ‖α=1\|\phi\|_{\alpha}=1,

‖[Sf1​(z)−Sf2​(z)]​ϕ​(z)‖α+42≤ε2​α+5α+1,\|[S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)]\phi(z)\|_{\alpha+4}^{2}\leq{\varepsilon}^{2}\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1},

and

(α+5)​∬Δ2​|Sf1​(z)−Sf2​(z)|​|Sf2​(z)|​|ϕ⁡(z)|2​(1−|z|2)α+4​d​x​d​yπ≤12​ε​α+5α+1.(\alpha+5)\iint_{\Delta}2|S_{f_{1}}(z)-S_{f_{2}}(z)||S_{f_{2}}(z)||\phi(z)|^{2}(1-|z|^{2})^{\alpha+4}\frac{dxdy}{\pi}\leq 12\varepsilon\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}.

It follows that

𝕄f12​(α)≤𝕄f22​(α)+ε2​α+5α+1+12​ε​α+5α+1.\mathbb{M}_{f_{1}}^{2}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{f_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)+{\varepsilon}^{2}\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}+12\varepsilon\frac{\alpha+5}{\alpha+1}.

For α>−1\alpha>-1, we define

𝕄⁡(α):=supf∈𝒮Q‖ℳf‖=supf∈𝒮Q𝕄f​(α).{\mathbb{M}}(\alpha):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}}\|\mathcal{M}_{f}\|=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}}\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha).

Then we have

Proposition 7.30.

For each α>−1\alpha>-1, we have 𝕄f​(α)<𝕄​(α)\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)<\mathbb{M}(\alpha) for any f∈𝒮Qf\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}.

Proof.

Let f∈𝒮Qf\in\mathcal{S}_{Q}. If ‖Sf‖E2=0\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}=0, then 𝕄f​(α)=0\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)=0 and the proposition holds. Next we will assume that ‖Sf‖E2>0\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}>0 so that 𝕄f​(α)>0\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)>0. Then we know from a classical result of the theory of universal Teichmüller space (see [3], [28]) that there is a constant δ>0\delta>0 such that 𝒪f:={φ∈𝒜⁡(Δ):‖φ−Sf‖E2<δ}\mathcal{O}_{f}:=\{\varphi\in\mathcal{A}(\Delta):\|\varphi-S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}<\delta\} is contained in 𝐒Q{\mathbf{S}}_{Q}, here, 𝐒Q{\mathbf{S}}_{Q} is defined as in (7.1). It follows that there is a function f0∈𝒮Qf_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{Q} such that Sf0=(1+δ2​‖Sf‖E2−1)​SfS_{f_{0}}=(1+\frac{\delta}{2}\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}^{-1})S_{f} since (1+δ2​‖Sf‖E2−1)​Sf(1+\frac{\delta}{2}\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}^{-1})S_{f} belongs to 𝒪f\mathcal{O}_{f}. Then

𝕄f0​(α)=(1+δ2​‖Sf‖E2−1)​𝕄f​(α)>𝕄f​(α).\mathbb{M}_{f_{0}}(\alpha)=(1+\frac{\delta}{2}\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}^{-1})\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)>\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha).

The proof of Proposition 7.30 is complete. ∎

Remark 7.31.

Proposition 7.29 and 7.30 suggest us that, for each α>−1\alpha>-1, if the biggest norm 𝕄⁡(α)\mathbb{M}(\alpha) can be attained at some point SfS_{f} in 𝐒¯Q\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{Q}, the closure of 𝐒Q\mathbf{S}_{Q}, then SfS_{f} must lie on ∂𝐒Q\partial\mathbf{S}_{Q}. However, we do not know the answer to the following problem.

Problem 7.32.

Can the functional Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} attain at least one maximum in 𝐒¯Q\overline{\mathbf{S}}_{Q} for each α>−1\alpha>-1?

Remark 7.33.

In light of Proposition 7.26, to find more functions satisfying the Brennan conjecture, it is natural to study the problem that in which subset of 𝒮\mathcal{S} the Koebe function and its rotations provide the biggest norm for the multiplication operator when α>0\alpha>0. That is

Problem 7.34.

For each α>0\alpha>0, which functions f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S} satisfy 𝕄f​(α)≤𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)?

It should be pointed out that it has been checked in [38] that for a large class of univalent functions ff belonging to 𝒮Q\mathcal{S}_{Q}, 𝕄f​(α)≤𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha) holds for each α>0\alpha>0.

Remark 7.35.

Let α>0,f∈𝒮\alpha>0,f\in\mathcal{S}. By checking carefully the arguments in the proof of Proposition 88 in [54, Page 1632], we see that, if there is a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that

𝕄f​(α)+𝕄f​(α+2)≤𝕄κ​(α)+𝕄κ​(α+2),\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)+\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha+2)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)+\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha+2),

for α∈(0,ε)\alpha\in(0,\varepsilon), then βf​(−2)≤1\beta_{f}({-2})\leq 1. Moreover, for R∈𝒰RR\in\mathcal{U}_{R} that have at least one critical point on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, if there are two small constants ϵ>0,η>0\epsilon>0,\eta>0 such that 𝕄R​(α)<𝕄κ​(α)−η\mathbb{M}_{R}(\alpha)<\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)-\eta for α∈(−ϵ,ϵ)∪(2−ϵ,2+ϵ)\alpha\in(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\cup(2-\epsilon,2+\epsilon), then we will obtain that βR​(−2)<1\beta_{R}(-2)<1, which is a contradiction. This leads us to conjecture that the following claim holds. Indeed, this is the case, and a proof of this claim can be found in [40].

Claim 7.36.

For each α>−1\alpha>-1, we have 𝕄R​(α)≥𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{R}(\alpha)\geq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha) for all R∈𝒰RR\in\mathcal{U}_{R} that have at least one critical point on 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Remark 7.37.

We have proved that, for each α>−1\alpha>-1,

𝕄ℰ22​(α)=𝕄P32​(α)=𝕄κ2​(α)=36​(α+3)​(α+5)(α+2)​(α+4).\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{2}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{P_{3}}^{2}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{2}(\alpha)=\frac{36(\alpha+3)(\alpha+5)}{(\alpha+2)(\alpha+4)}.

It is interesting to consider the following

Problem 7.38.

For each α>−1\alpha>-1, which functions f∈𝒰Rf\in\mathcal{U}_{R} satisfy 𝕄f​(α)=𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha)?

Remark 7.39.

If our guess that Problem 7.34 has an affirmative answer for every ff in 𝒮\mathcal{S} is true, i.e., 𝕄f​(α)≤𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha) holds for every α>0\alpha>0 and all f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S}, then the Brennan conjecture follows. Furthermore, since Claim 7.36 holds, it follows that 𝕄R​(α)=𝕄κ​(α)\mathbb{M}_{R}(\alpha)=\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}(\alpha) for every α>0\alpha>0 and all R∈𝒰RR\in\mathcal{U}_{R} that have at least one critical point on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Although these predictions may seem surprising, no counterexamples are known to the author. Finally, based on the above findings, we further conjecture that

Conjecture 7.40.

For every α>0\alpha>0, if the functional Λα\Lambda_{\alpha} attains the maximum on SfS_{f} in 𝐒¯\overline{\mathbf{S}} for some f∈𝒮f\in\mathcal{S}, then ‖Sf‖E2=6\|S_{f}\|_{E_{2}}=6.
